description: Six individually checked observational and documentary images with rights: gold STM, archaeal electron micrograph, DNA AFM, live neuronal network, anatomical ear model and 1973 EPA classroom photograph.

images.title: Atomic structure on a gold surface
images.summary: A scanning tunneling microscopy measurement of the reconstructed Au(100) surface reveals individual gold atoms in closely spaced ridges, observed by Erwin Rossen at Eindhoven University of Technology.
images.alt: Gold and rust-toned banded image consisting of parallel elevated rows with a granular pattern at atomic scale.
images.caption: An STM electronic measurement visualizes the atomic lattice on clean gold, with contrast and shading assigned by the instrument. It is not a visible-light photograph or a literal picture taken with an ordinary camera.
images.credit: Erwin Rossen / Eindhoven University of Technology
images.rights: Photographer/experimenter Erwin Rossen released this image to the public domain worldwide as documented at the Commons file page.
images.processing: Observed source image converted to a maximum 1800-pixel-wide quality-87 JPEG for the development archive. Source original retained by URL; no generated imagery or edits of scientific structures. Original instrument color mapping preserved.

images.title: Electron micrograph of a methane-producing archaeon
images.summary: A single Methanococcus maripaludis archaeal cell with thin surface filaments, or archaella, observed by electron microscopy. The original includes a 500-nanometer scale bar.
images.alt: Gray electron micrograph showing one roughly round dark cell with many very thin hairlike filaments extending from its surface.
images.caption: An archaeon is neither a bacterium nor a eukaryote. This real electron micrograph shows Methanococcus maripaludis and its motility structures. The bright-and-dark contrast is an electron imaging signal, not natural color.
images.credit: Dr. Ken F. Jarrell and Dr. Shin-Ichi Aizawa
images.rights: CC0 1.0 dedication recorded on Commons for this contributed research image. The named researchers are credited; independently verify downstream rights before any hardware archival publication.
images.processing: Observed source image converted to a maximum 1800-pixel-wide quality-87 JPEG for the development archive. Source original retained by URL; no generated imagery or edits of scientific structures. Electron microscope grayscale retained.

images.title: DNA molecules in a nanotechnology array
images.summary: Atomic force microscopy measurement of DNA double-crossover structures arranged on mica; the field width is 150 nanometers. Individual DX molecules are visible in the array.
images.alt: Gold-orange rectangular field containing repeated small DNA-structure signals against dark rust-red background.
images.caption: DNA molecular structures measured using atomic force microscopy, arranged as an artificial nanotechnology lattice on mica. This is not a direct microscope photograph of the entire genetic molecule inside a living cell.
images.rights: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported (CC BY-SA 3.0), © Antony-22. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/ . Re-encoded archive derivative licensed identically with attribution and processing disclosed.
images.processing: Observed source image converted to a maximum 1800-pixel-wide quality-87 JPEG for the development archive. Source original retained by URL; no generated imagery or edits of scientific structures. Original false-color instrument visualization retained.

images.title: Cultured neurons forming a network
images.summary: A label-free holotomography observation of rat cortical neurons on day 14 in a laboratory culture, visualizing cell bodies and connecting neurites.
images.alt: Gray and black microscopy field showing a complex web of slender neuron projections connecting numerous round cellular bodies, with a small 20-micrometer scale bar.
images.caption: Live cultured rat neurons observed by holotomography without fluorescent labeling. This illustrates neural tissue at a cellular scale, not the human brain or a complete nervous system.
images.rights: CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication by the creator, documented on the Wikimedia Commons file page.
images.processing: Observed source image converted to a maximum 1800-pixel-wide quality-87 JPEG for the development archive. Source original retained by URL; no generated imagery or edits of scientific structures. Holotomography grayscale and 20-micrometer scale retained.

images.title: The ear's sound pathway shown in a teaching model
images.summary: A real photograph of a large anatomical teaching model of the human ear at the Museum of Veterinary Anatomy, University of São Paulo, showing the outer ear, ear canal, eardrum, ossicles, cochlea and semicircular canals.
images.alt: A physical sectional model of an ear on a table, showing the outer pinna at left, internal ossicle parts in the middle and a spiral cochlea on the right.
images.caption: A photographed educational model, not living tissue. Sound vibration normally travels from the outer ear to the eardrum and middle-ear bones, then the fluid-filled cochlea; actual anatomy is more complex than this representation.
images.credit: Museum of Veterinary Anatomy FMVZ USP / Wagner Souza e Silva
images.rights: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0), institution-approved. Credit must read Museum of Veterinary Anatomy FMVZ USP / Wagner Souza e Silva, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/. Resized derivative remains CC BY-SA 4.0.

images.title: Students participate in a Texas classroom
images.summary: A 1973 US Environmental Protection Agency DOCUMERICA photograph by Marc St. Gil shows students in a classroom in Leakey, Texas. Two students raise their hands while another student is shown from behind.
images.alt: A warm-toned color archival image of two school students raising hands beside wooden desks in a classroom with books and papers.
images.caption: An ordinary classroom interaction in Leakey, Texas, 1973, documented by EPA photographer Marc St. Gil. This is one historic educational setting; publication does not establish whether the subjects gave separate model-release consent.
images.credit: Marc St. Gil / US Environmental Protection Agency, DOCUMERICA
images.rights: US federal employee work, public domain in the United States under 17 USC 105, recorded on Wikimedia Commons source page. Subjects were minors; editorial/privacy review is still required before additional promotional use.
images.processing: Observed source image converted to a maximum 1800-pixel-wide quality-87 JPEG for the development archive. Source original retained by URL; no generated imagery or edits of scientific structures. The original archival color balance and composition are preserved.
